title: Advanced Feature Engineering and Feature Stores
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Advanced Feature Engineering and Feature Stores ##### 0.91 offline, 0.63 in production A ride-hailing company in Bengaluru built a surge-pricing model. Offline AUC: 0.91. Two weeks after launch, measured online: 0.63. The investigation took nine days. The training pipeline computed `driver_avg_rating_30d` from the analytics warehouse using a SQL window over the last 30 days *relative to each historical trip*. The serving path computed it from a Redis cache that a separate Node.js service updated — and that service used a 30-day window ending at *midnight*, plus it counted cancelled trips, which the SQL version excluded. Two teams, two implementations, same feature name, different numbers. The model had learned relationships that simply did not exist at inference time. This is **training/serving skew**, and it is the most expensive recurring bug in applied ML. Today covers the feature techniques that make models good, and the infrastructure that stops those features from silently diverging. ##### Target encoding, done safely Target encoding replaces a categorical value with the mean target for that category. It is enormously powerful for high-cardinality features — `pincode`, `merchant_id`, `device_model` — where one-hot encoding creates 40,000 sparse columns. It is also the most common source of leakage in tabular ML, because the naive version uses each row's own target to build its own feature. ```python # WRONG — every row's target leaks into its own encoding df["city_te"] = df.groupby("city")["target"].transform("mean") ``` On a category with one row, that feature *is* the label. The model finds it instantly, validation looks brilliant, production collapses. The fix is **cross-fitting** — encode each fold using only the other folds — combined with **smoothing** toward the global mean so rare categories are not trusted: ```python import numpy as np, pandas as pd from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin from sklearn.model_selection import KFold class TargetEncoder(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin): """Leakage-safe target encoding: out-of-fold during fit, full-data at transform.""" def __init__(self, cols, n_splits=5, smoothing=20.0, random_state=42): self.cols, self.n_splits = cols, n_splits self.smoothing, self.random_state = smoothing, random_state def _encode(self, stats, prior): # Empirical Bayes shrinkage toward the global mean return (stats["sum"] + prior * self.smoothing) / (stats["count"] + self.smoothing) def fit(self, X, y): y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) self.prior_ = y.mean() self.maps_ = {} for c in self.cols: stats = pd.DataFrame({"v": X[c].values, "y": y}).groupby("v")["y"].agg(["sum", "count"]) self.maps_[c] = self._encode(stats, self.prior_) return self def fit_transform(self, X, y): y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float) self.fit(X, y) out = X.copy() kf = KFold(self.n_splits, shuffle=True, random_state=self.random_state) for c in self.cols: oof = np.full(len(X), self.prior_) for tr_idx, va_idx in kf.split(X): stats = (pd.DataFrame({"v": X[c].values[tr_idx], "y": y[tr_idx]}) .groupby("v")["y"].agg(["sum", "count"])) m = self._encode(stats, y[tr_idx].mean()) oof[va_idx] = X[c].values[va_idx].astype(object) oof[va_idx] = pd.Series(X[c].values[va_idx]).map(m).fillna(self.prior_).values out[c + "_te"] = oof return out.drop(columns=self.cols) def transform(self, X): out = X.copy() for c in self.cols: out[c + "_te"] = X[c].map(self.maps_[c]).fillna(self.prior_) return out.drop(columns=self.cols) ``` Two details that matter: `fit_transform` produces out-of-fold values for training, while `transform` uses full-data statistics for validation and serving — this asymmetry is the point. And unseen categories at serving time must fall back to the prior, never to NaN. **Frequency encoding** is the safer cousin: replace a category with its occurrence count. It uses no target information at all, so it cannot leak, and it captures the "rare categories behave differently" signal surprisingly well. Compute the counts on training data only and persist the map. ##### Time-series features: lags, rolling, and the point-in-time rule Every temporal feature must obey one rule: **as of timestamp `t`, use only information available before `t`.** Violating it is the second great leakage family. ```python def build_temporal_features(df, id_col="user_id", ts_col="ts", val="amount_inr"): df = df.sort_values([id_col, ts_col]).copy() g = df.groupby(id_col, observed=True)[val] # Lags: strictly past values for k in (1, 2, 3, 7): df[f"lag_{k}"] = g.shift(k) # Rolling stats — shift(1) FIRST so the current row is excluded shifted = g.shift(1) for w in (7, 30): r = shifted.groupby(df[id_col], observed=True).rolling(w, min_periods=2) df[f"roll{w}_mean"] = r.mean().reset_index(level=0, drop=True) df[f"roll{w}_std"] = r.std().reset_index(level=0, drop=True) # Expanding (all history to date) df["expanding_mean"] = shifted.groupby(df[id_col], observed=True).expanding().mean() \ .reset_index(level=0, drop=True) # Momentum / trend ratios df["momentum"] = df["roll7_mean"] / df["roll30_mean"].replace(0, np.nan) # Recency and calendar df["days_since_prev"] = g.transform(lambda s: s.index.to_series().diff()).fillna(-1) ts = df[ts_col].dt.tz_convert("Asia/Kolkata") df["hour"] = ts.dt.hour df["dow"] = ts.dt.dayofweek df["is_month_end"] = ts.dt.is_month_end.astype(int) # Cyclical encoding: hour 23 and hour 0 should be adjacent df["hour_sin"] = np.sin(2 * np.pi * df["hour"] / 24) df["hour_cos"] = np.cos(2 * np.pi * df["hour"] / 24) return df ``` The `shift(1)` before `rolling` is non-negotiable. And validation must be temporal — `TimeSeriesSplit` or an explicit date cutoff, never `train_test_split(shuffle=True)`, which lets the model train on next week and test on last week. ##### Automated feature engineering Tools like **Featuretools** apply Deep Feature Synthesis: given entity relationships, they generate aggregations (`MEAN(transactions.amount BY user)`) and transforms recursively across a defined depth. ```python import featuretools as ft es = ft.EntitySet(id="fintech") es = es.add_dataframe("users", users, index="user_id") es = es.add_dataframe("txns", txns, index="txn_id", time_index="ts") es = es.add_relationship("users", "user_id", "txns", "user_id") fm, defs = ft.dfs( entityset=es, target_dataframe_name="users", agg_primitives=["mean", "sum", "std", "count", "num_unique", "trend"], trans_primitives=["day", "month", "weekend"], cutoff_time=cutoff_df, # ESSENTIAL: enforces point-in-time correctness max_depth=2, ) ``` `cutoff_time` is what separates a useful tool from a leakage generator. Without it, DFS happily aggregates future rows. The honest assessment: automated FE is good for breadth-first exploration and hackathon speed, and it generates hundreds of features you must then prune. Domain knowledge still wins — "ratio of night-time UPI transactions to total" is a feature no primitive will invent. ##### Scaling and transformation pipelines The rule that prevents subtle leakage: **fit scalers on training data only, inside a pipeline.** ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, QuantileTransformer, OneHotEncoder from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer numeric = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True)), ("scale", QuantileTransformer(output_distribution="normal", n_quantiles=1000)), ]) categorical = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="__missing__")), ("ohe", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="infrequent_if_exist", min_frequency=0.01)), ]) pre = ColumnTransformer([("num", numeric, num_cols), ("cat", categorical, cat_cols)]) ``` Which scaler: `StandardScaler` for roughly Gaussian features, `RobustScaler` when outliers dominate, `QuantileTransformer` for arbitrary skew (it is what tames rupee amounts spanning ₹10 to ₹10 lakh), and `PowerTransformer` when you want an interpretable monotone transform. Tree models need none of these — but they do need the same *imputation* logic in training and serving. `add_indicator=True` on the imputer is underrated: missingness is often signal, and dropping it discards information. ##### Feature stores and the anti-skew architecture A feature store is a system that computes each feature **once**, from **one definition**, and serves it to both training (historical, point-in-time correct) and inference (fresh, low-latency). ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Raw sources: Postgres, Kafka, S3] --> B[Feature definitions - one Python file] B --> C[Materialization job] C --> D[(Offline store: Parquet / BigQuery)] C --> E[(Online store: Redis / DynamoDB)] D -->|get_historical_features
point-in-time join| F[Training job] E -->|get_online_features
single-digit ms| G[Prediction API] F --> H[Model artifact] H --> G ``` In Feast, the definition is the contract: ```python from feast import Entity, FeatureView, Field, FileSource from feast.types import Float32, Int64 from datetime import timedelta user = Entity(name="user", join_keys=["user_id"]) source = FileSource(path="s3://calibi/features/user_stats.parquet", timestamp_field="event_timestamp") user_stats = FeatureView( name="user_stats", entities=[user], ttl=timedelta(days=7), schema=[ Field(name="txn_count_30d", dtype=Int64), Field(name="avg_amount_30d", dtype=Float32), Field(name="days_since_signup", dtype=Int64), ], source=source, online=True, ) ``` ```python # Training — point-in-time correct join against an entity/timestamp dataframe train_df = store.get_historical_features( entity_df=labels_df[["user_id", "event_timestamp", "churned"]], features=["user_stats:txn_count_30d", "user_stats:avg_amount_30d"], ).to_df() # Serving — same names, same definition, milliseconds vec = store.get_online_features( features=["user_stats:txn_count_30d", "user_stats:avg_amount_30d"], entity_rows=[{"user_id": "u_1042"}], ).to_dict() ``` The **point-in-time join** is the feature store's core value: for a label at 2026-03-14 09:00, it retrieves the feature values as they were *at that instant*, not today's values. Doing this correctly by hand in SQL is possible (`ASOF JOIN` in DuckDB, a correlated lateral join in Postgres) but easy to get wrong across dozens of features. **Do you need Feast?** Not always. If a single Python module computes features and both paths import it, you have solved 80% of skew for 2% of the cost. Adopt a store when you have multiple models sharing features, streaming freshness requirements, or several teams — the operational overhead (a registry, a materialization scheduler, an online store) is real. Regardless, add a skew *detector*: log a sample of production feature vectors, recompute the same rows offline, and alert on any mismatch beyond tolerance. That check would have found the Bengaluru bug on day one instead of day fourteen. ##### Common mistakes - Target encoding without cross-fitting — the single most common leakage bug in tabular ML. - No smoothing, so a category with two rows gets a fully-trusted encoding. - Rolling windows that include the current row. - `train_test_split(shuffle=True)` on temporal data. - Fitting the scaler on the full dataset before splitting. - Two implementations of "the same" feature in two languages. - Serving without a fallback for unseen categorical values. - Automated feature synthesis without `cutoff_time`. - Hour-of-day as a raw integer, so 23 and 0 are maximally distant. - Deploying a feature store and still letting one team compute features on the side. ##### Hands-on Build the leakage-safe target encoder above and prove it works: train once with the naive version and once with cross-fitting, and show the naive version's validation AUC is inflated while its test-on-future AUC is worse. Then engineer a full temporal feature set — lags, shifted rolling stats, momentum, recency, cyclical calendar encodings — for a forecasting dataset and validate with `TimeSeriesSplit`. For the mini-project, stand up a minimal Feast repo: one entity, one feature view, `feast apply`, `feast materialize`, then fetch the *same* feature for the *same* entity through both `get_historical_features` and `get_online_features` and assert the values match. Write your training/serving-skew explanation around a concrete case — the 30-day-window mismatch above is a good template — and describe exactly which part of the feature-store architecture eliminates it. ##### Key takeaways - Target encoding needs out-of-fold fitting plus smoothing, or it leaks the label directly into the feature. - Every temporal feature must obey point-in-time correctness; `shift(1)` before every rolling window. - Fit scalers and imputers inside a pipeline on training folds only — never on the full dataset. - Training/serving skew comes from two implementations of one feature; a shared definition is the cure. - A feature store's real product is the point-in-time join and one definition serving both paths — adopt it when scale justifies the operational cost.
